subject: British History
title: 2. The Hanoverian Era: Jacobites, Walpole and American Independence

segments.text: This topic covers three connected developments — securing the Protestant succession, developing cabinet government, and losing the American colonies — that together show both the consolidation and the limits of Britain’s post-1688 constitutional and imperial settlement.

items.text: The movement seeking to restore the exiled Catholic Stuart line, defeated decisively at Culloden in 1746.
The dominance of Whig elites in eighteenth-century political life through parliamentary influence and patronage.
Make three mini-topics: Hanoverian succession/Jacobitism; Walpole and political institutions; the American crisis.
For Walpole, explain why he is often called Britain’s first prime minister while noting the office evolved gradually rather than being formally created.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “How did the constitutional dispute over taxation without representation escalate into American independence?”
Do not say Walpole legally created the office of prime minister; the office evolved through convention.
Do not explain the American Revolution only through taxation; representation, imperial authority, colonial institutions and Enlightenment ideas all mattered.
Do not assume the loss of America ended the British Empire; imperial expansion continued elsewhere (Topic 5).
George I became king in 1714 under the Protestant succession established by earlier legislation.
Major Jacobite risings occurred in 1715 and 1745; the latter ended decisively after Culloden in 1746.
Robert Walpole dominated government from 1721 to 1742 and helped develop cabinet-parliamentary practices.
Britain’s victory in the Seven Years’ War increased imperial territory but also debt, contributing to disputes over taxing the American colonies.
The Treaty of Paris (1783) confirmed British recognition of American independence.
Jacobite defeat, Walpole’s political management, and the American crisis together show the Hanoverian era consolidating domestic constitutional order while exposing the limits of imperial control.
The American dispute is best explained as a genuine constitutional disagreement (representation and consent to taxation), not merely a tax-rate grievance.
Loss of America directly caused Britain’s later imperial reorientation toward Asia, the Pacific and Africa, examined in Topic 5.
